catalog_quote: The prosody of Huajuapan has been analyzed by Pike & Cowan (1967). P&C observe that there are three tones in this language (H, M, and L), and every vowel bears one and only one tone. Syllables have the shape (C)(C)V, and all possible tone sequences are attested. Primary stress falls on either the root or its suffixes, and never on prefixes. There are no secondary stresses. Huajuapan’s stress system is described by P&C (p.17) as follows (only representative examples are given here for reasons of brevity. For a fuller list, see Appendix 1): (17) (i) Stress the leftmost syllable which is followed by a syllable with a lower tone. HH+L: sádí+nà ‘he/she/they (known) are closing it’ MM+L: nì-so ni+nà ‘he/she/they (known) tied it’ H+ML: kó+ naà ‘a wide thing’ M+LH: ña+nìní ‘your (sg, adult) brother’ (ii) Otherwise stress the leftmost syllable. H+HH: sá+díní ‘you (sg, adult) are not closing (it)’ M+MM: nì-ke+en do ‘you (pl) teased (someone)’ ... L+MM: šì+toso ‘our (incl.) bed’ ... So, ... sequences (abbreviated henceforth to HL, HM, ML) are sought out, and stress falls on the first syllable of such sequences. If there are no such sequences, stress falls on the initial syllable of the PrWd.

new_statements.quote: In Huajuapan Mixtec, E. Pike and Cowan (1967) also identify the couplet as an important unit, with stress on the first syllable of the couplet unless there is a following syllable within the word with a lower tone; in that case, word stress occurs on the syllable preceding the lower tone; stress never precedes the couplet. Tones are mostly predictable on non-stem morphemes.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Three-tone language (high, mid, low) with one word stress per phonological word. Default: stress on the first syllable of the couplet (the bimoraic stem nucleus, i.e. stem-initial). Tone-conditioned shift: if a later syllable within the word (couplet or post-couplet enclitic) bears a lower tone than what precedes it, stress falls on the syllable immediately before that lower tone (first syllable of a falling tone sequence). Pre-couplet (prefix) syllables are never stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned in the second-hand reports.
new_statements.exceptions: The tone-conditioned rightward shift itself; stress never on pre-couplet syllables. Carroll 2015:92 groups Huajuapan with Ayutla/Molinos/Mixtepec as 'tone-dependent stress' where 'the preferred stress position is the first syllable of a falling tone sequence, and the default position is the first syllable of the couplet'.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word = couplet plus following (post-couplet/enclitic) syllables; prefixes excluded. Statement is second-hand; the primary (Pike & Cowan 1967:7) was not accessible, so exact wording, examples and whether the shift is described as loudness vs. pitch prominence (cf. Mortensen's remark on Ayutla) remain unverified.
new_statements.identity_note: Pike & Cowan's 'Huajuapan Mixtec' is the variety of Santiago Cacaloxtepec near Huajuapan de Leon, Oaxaca = Cacaloxtepec Mixtec [miu], Glottolog caca1250: SIL archive entry 2459 tags the article 'Subject Languages: Cacaloxtepec Mixtec [miu]'; Glottolog's bib gives language code 'Huajuapan = Cacaloxtepec Mixtec [miu]'; Josserand 1983 equates 'Huajuapan de Leon-Oaxaca = Cacaloxtepec'. Glottolog/ELCat also list 'Tezoatlan Mixtec' as an alternative name, but Ethnologue's Tezoatlan Mixtec is a separate code [mxb]; the statement here concerns [miu] only.

tone_statements.quote: Santiago Cacaloxtepec Mixtec The data for this variety come from Dürr (1987). There are three level tones (low, mid, high), but the high and mid tone never combine, resulting in 7 contrastive tone melodies. The lost final glottal stop has a lowering effect, resulting in a merger of the low tone sets. *H generally has a mid tone reflex and *L a low tone. There is a further merger of HL with the HHʔ set. Table 44: Contrastive tone melodies in Cacaloxtepec Mixtec 1.1 3.1 5.1 / 1.3 3.3 / 1.5 5.5

tone_statements.quote: Un sistema tonal muy elaborado es una de las características del mixteco. La tonología comparativa muestra una diversificación dialectal muy pronunciada ... El artículo trata de reconstruir el sistema tonal del protomixteco. Cada morfema tenía una combinación de dos tonos: *alto-alto, *alto-bajo, *bajo-bajo y *bajo-alto. Además, el cierre glotal final, hoy desaparecido en la mayoría de los dialectos, se ha manifestado en cambios detono.
tone_statements.translation: A very elaborate tonal system is one of the characteristics of Mixtec. Comparative tonology shows a very pronounced dialectal diversification ... The article attempts to reconstruct the tonal system of Proto-Mixtec. Each morpheme had a combination of two tones: *high-high, *high-low, *low-low and *low-high. In addition, the final glottal stop, today lost in most dialects, has shown up as tone changes.
tone_statements.summary: Proto-Mixtec *HH *HL *LL *LH (+ *-ʔ) > Cacaloxtepec 3 level tones, 7 couplet melodies (per Auderset's reading of Dürr's data).

sources.note: Cacaloxtepec Mixtec (data from Dürr 1987) has three level tones low/mid/high; high and mid never combine within the couplet, giving 7 contrastive tone melodies (Chao digits 1.1 3.1 5.1 / 1.3 3.3 / 1.5 5.5); the lost final glottal stop has a lowering effect merging the low-tone sets; *H generally > mid, *L > low; HL merges with the HHʔ set. Crossref abstract of the article: tests whether tones change faster / carry less phylogenetic signal than segments across Mixtec varieties using coded tone changes (this variety is one of the 42-43 coded).

sources.quote: Un sistema tonal muy elaborado es una de las características del mixteco. La tonología comparativa muestra una diversificación dialectal muy pronunciada ... El artículo trata de reconstruir el sistema tonal del protomixteco. Cada morfema tenía una combinación de dos tonos: *alto-alto, *alto-bajo, *bajo-bajo y *bajo-alto. sources.note: Reconstructs the Proto-Mixtec tonal system - every morpheme carried one of four two-tone combinations *high-high, *high-low, *low-low, *low-high, and the final glottal stop, now lost in most dialects, surfaces as tone changes; dialect differences are explained from this reconstruction.
